Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:17: Further, the ways of repentance are learned from the repentance of Ahab, as explained in Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer (chapter 42), in these words: Rabbi Akiva says, repentance was created, and the right hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, is stretched out to receive penitents every day, and He says, return, sons of men. Know the power of charity and repentance - come and see from Ahab, king of Israel, who did great repentance, for he robbed, was violent, and murdered, as it is said (1 Kings 21:19), "have you murdered, and also taken possession?" He sent and called Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and would give himself forty lashes three times every day, and in fasting and prayer he would rise early and stay late before the Holy One, blessed be He, and would occupy himself with Torah all his days, and did not return to his evil deeds again - and his repentance was accepted, as it is said (ibid. 21:29), "have you seen how Ahab humbles himself before Me?" and so on - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:18: And further they said in the Pesikta (D'Rav Kahana, pesikta 24), concerning Ahab's repentance: he was accustomed to eat at the third hour of the day; [instead] he would eat at the fourth hour; [and one who normally ate] at the seventh hour, would eat at the ninth hour. And so they said in the Pesikta (ibid.), "and went softly" (1 Kings 21:27) - that he walked barefoot - and we copied his words above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:19: Further, the ways of repentance are learned from the repentance of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish. He said there in Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer: Ben Azzai says, come and see the power of repentance from Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who, together with his two companions, would rob and take by violence from anyone who passed them on the road. What did he do? He left his two companions robbing in the mountains and returned to the God of his fathers with all his heart, in fasting and prayer, rising early and staying late before the Holy One, blessed be He, and occupying himself with Torah all his days and with gifts to the poor, and did not return to his evil deeds again - and his repentance was accepted. And on the day he died, his robber companions in the mountains also died, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish was given a portion of life, while his two companions went to the depths of Sheol; and both of them said before the Holy One, blessed be He, is there favoritism before You? This one robbed with us in the mountains, and he is in the treasury of life, while we are in the depths of Sheol! He said to them, this one repented in his lifetime, and you did not. They said to him, leave us and we will repent. He said to them, there is no repentance except until death. To what may this be compared? To a person who wishes to journey by sea - if he does not take bread with him from an inhabited land, he will not find any at sea; if he wishes to go to the edge of the desert, if he does not take bread and water with him from a settled place, he will find nothing to eat or drink in the desert. So too, if a person does not repent in his lifetime, after death he has no repentance, as it is said, "who will not show favoritism," and it is written (Proverbs 6:35), "he will not regard any ransom," and it is written (Jeremiah 17:10), "I, the LORD, search the heart, I test the kidneys" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:20: We learn from the general discourse of Reish Lakish's repentance five things required for repentance: the first, fasting; the second, prayer; the third, rising early and staying late at the synagogue; the fourth, occupation with Torah; the fifth, charity. And these things, when combined with one another, atone for iniquities and tear up one's sentence.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:21: Fasting is fitting for repentance, as it is written (Joel 2:12), "return to Me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:22: And likewise prayer is needed for repentance - prayer from the depths of the heart - and so they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, end of page 69), on the verse (Psalms 130:1), "out of the depths I have cried to You, O LORD." He says: when is a person purified of his sin? At the hour he enters into this repentance as is fitting. Rabbi Yitzchak said, that he returns before the supernal King and prays a prayer from the depths of his heart - this is what is written, "out of the depths I have cried to You, O LORD" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:23: And further, in Vayikra Rabbah (10:5), the Tannaim disagree on this: Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi said, prayer does everything - from whom do you learn this? From Chizkiyahu - the essence of his reign was only fourteen years, as it is said (2 Kings 18:13), "and in the fourteenth year of King Chizkiyahu," and since he prayed, fifteen more years were added to him, as it is said (Isaiah 38:5), "behold, I will add to your days fifteen years." Rabbi Yehoshua says, prayer accomplishes half - from whom do you learn this? From Aaron, against whom a harsh decree was decreed, as it is said (Deuteronomy 9:20), "and the LORD was very angry with Aaron to have destroyed him" - and "destruction" [hashmadah] means nothing other than the loss of children, along the lines of (Amos 2:9), "and I destroyed his fruit from above and his roots from beneath" - and since Moses prayed, two [sons] died and two remained - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:24: And further, they elaborated on the virtue of prayer in Tractate Berachot (32b), in these words: Rabbi Elazar said, prayer is greater than good deeds, for there is none greater in good deeds than Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, and nevertheless he was answered only through prayer, as it is said (Deuteronomy 3:26), "speak no more to Me of this matter" - and adjacent to it, "go up to the top of Pisgah" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:25: And in Vayikra Rabbah (30:3), on the verse "and you shall take for yourselves on the first day" (Leviticus 23:40), he explained the verse (Psalms 102:18), "He has regarded the prayer of the destitute [ha-ar'ar]" as referring to the prayer of Menasheh. And afterward he says: Rabbi Yitzchak interpreted the verse as applying to these generations, who have neither king, nor prophet, nor priest, nor Urim and Tummim, and have nothing but this prayer alone. David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, do not despise their prayer. "Let this be written for the last generation" - from here that the Holy One, blessed be He, accepts penitents. "And a people yet to be created shall praise the LORD" - that the Holy One, blessed be He, creates them as a new creature - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:26: And in the Yerushalmi (Tractate Rosh Hashanah, chapter 2, halachah 5), concerning the sons of Eli, of whom it is said (1 Samuel 3:14), "if it shall be atoned for," and so on, "with sacrifice and offering" - it is explained there that with sacrifice and offering he is not atoned, but he is atoned through prayer.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:27: Rising early and staying late at the synagogue - it is said in Tanna D'Vei Eliyahu (Rabbah, chapter 21), on the verse (Numbers 24:6), "as valleys are they spread forth, as gardens by the river's side" - what have valleys/streams to do with synagogues and study halls? Rather, just as people descend into these streams while impure, and immerse and emerge pure, so too people enter synagogues and study halls full of iniquities, and emerge full of commandments - to this point. And there are further, many virtues in rising early and staying late, to be explained in its place, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:28: Torah atones for iniquity - this is well known. And likewise charity, part of the commandment of acts of kindness, and it is written (Proverbs 16:6), "by kindness and truth iniquity is atoned for" - and they said in Rosh Hashanah (18a) that even a decree accompanied by an oath is nullified through occupation with Torah and acts of kindness, in these words: with sacrifice and offering he is not atoned, but he is atoned through Torah and acts of kindness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:29: And further they said in Vayikra Rabbah (parashah 25), on the verse "and you shall plant every tree for food" (Leviticus 19:23), in these words: Rav Huna said, if a person stumbles into a transgression liable for death by the hand of Heaven, what shall he do to live? If he was accustomed to read one page [of Scripture], let him read two pages; if he was accustomed to study one chapter [of Mishnah], let him study two chapters; and if he is not accustomed to reading and studying, what shall he do to live? Let him go and become a leader of the community and a charity treasurer, and he shall live - for had it been said, "cursed is he who does not study," there would be no recovery; rather, "cursed is he who does not fulfill" (Deuteronomy 27:26). Had it been said, "it is a tree of life to those who labor in it," there would be no recovery; rather, "it is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it" (Proverbs 3:18) - to this point. Behold, these two attributes were in Reish Lakish, which are the essence of atonement for iniquities, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:30: And further, the things mentioned diminish a person's decreed sentence - and so they said in Midrash Kohelet (5:4), "for in the multitude of dreams and vanities there are also many words; but fear God" (Ecclesiastes 5:6) - Rabbi said, if you have seen harsh dreams and harsh, disturbing visions, or you fear them, hasten to three things and you will be saved - for Rabbi Yudan said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, three things nullify evil decrees: prayer, charity, and repentance, and all three are in one verse (2 Chronicles 7:14), "and My people, who are called by My name, humble themselves and pray and seek My face, and turn from their evil ways, then I will hear from heaven and forgive their sin." "And pray" - this is prayer. "And seek My face" - this is charity, this is what is written (Psalms 17:15), "I, in righteousness [tzedek], shall behold Your face." "And turn from their evil ways" - this is repentance - and afterward, "and I will hear from heaven." Rabbi Muna says, also fasting, as it is said (ibid. 20:2), "may the LORD answer you in the day of trouble." Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yosi say, also change of name, change of deed, and change of place - to this point, relevant here - and all of these they proved there from verses, and the discourse is brought in Bereshit Rabbah (parashah 44:12).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:31: They said (Rosh Hashanah 16b): four things tear up a person's decreed sentence: charity, crying out [in prayer], change of name, and change of deed. Crying out, as it is written (Psalms 107:6), "then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and He brought them out of their distresses." Charity, as it is written (Proverbs 10:2), "but charity delivers from death." Change of deed, as it is written (Jonah 3:10), "and God saw their deeds." And some say, also change of place - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:32: And a penitent must increase in charity, as it is said (Daniel 4:24), "and break off your sin by righteousness" - and the reason is that corresponding to what he diminished the flow above, he must increase it - and especially on a fast day, as it is written in Isaiah (58:7), "is it not to share your bread with the hungry," and so on, referring to the fast.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:33: Further, for repentance one needs sackcloth, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 69:12), "and I made sackcloth my garment." And in Bereshit Rabbah (Parashat Vayeshev, parashah 84), our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said, on the verse "and Reuben returned to the pit" - and where had he been? Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua [disagree]. Rabbi Eliezer says, occupied with his sackcloth and his fast - once he had finished, he went and peered into that pit; this is what is written, "and Reuben returned to the pit." Rabbi Yehoshua says, all the burdens of the household were cast upon him, and once he was free of his household duties, he went and peered into that pit; this is what is written, "and Reuben returned to the pit." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, never before has a person sinned before Me and repented - and you opened with repentance first; by your life, a descendant of your descendants shall stand and open with repentance first - and who is this? Hosea, as it is said (Hosea 14:2), "return, O Israel, to the LORD your God" - and Rabbi Eliezer's words are more accepted in the Zohar. Behold, that repentance is [performed] through fasting and sackcloth.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:34: And further there, Rabbi Abahu said: because Jacob our father took hold of sackcloth, it has not departed from his sons and his sons' sons to the end of all generations - but it applies only to the great among men: David, as it is said (1 Chronicles 21:16), "then David and the elders fell upon their faces, covered in sackcloth"; Ahab, "and he put sackcloth upon his flesh" (1 Kings 21:27); Jehoram, "and the people looked, and behold, the sackcloth was upon his flesh" (2 Kings 6:30); Mordechai, "and put on sackcloth and ashes" (Esther 4:1) - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:35: And further, in Bereshit Rabbah, on the verse "and it came to pass at that time, that Judah went down" (parashah 85), in these words: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani opened (Jeremiah 29:11), "for I know the thoughts" - the tribes were occupied with the selling of Joseph, and Joseph was occupied with his sackcloth and his fast; Reuben was occupied with his sackcloth and his fast; and Jacob was occupied with his sackcloth and his fast - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:36: And further, in Midrash Rabbah, Parashat Vezot HaBerachah, they said, in these words: when Moses saw that a decree had been sealed against him, he decreed a fast, and drew a small circle and stood within it, and said, I will not move from here until that decree is nullified. At that hour, what did Moses do? He put on sackcloth and wrapped himself in sackcloth and rolled in ashes, and stood in prayer and supplication before the Omnipresent, until heaven and earth and the orders of creation trembled - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:37: And further they said in the Midrash (Yalkut Esther, section 1056), on the verse (Esther 4:4), "and she sent garments to clothe Mordechai, and to take away his sackcloth from him, but he did not accept them," in these words: he said, I will not remove the sackcloth until the Holy One, blessed be He, performs miracles with me as He did for the earlier ones - with Jacob it is written, "and he put sackcloth on his loins"; and with Ahab, [the punishment] was suspended for three years; and likewise with Jehoram, the famine in Samaria did not end while his sackcloth [remained].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:38: And I heard from the Kabbalists that "sak" [sackcloth] equals four hundred in numerical value - and the matter is that there are four hundred bands among the husks, of whom it is said concerning Esau (Genesis 32:6), "and four hundred men with him"; and above there are four hundred worlds of mercy, as explained at the beginning of the Idra (Parashat Naso, page 128b) - and through the wearing of sackcloth, one merits to subdue the four hundred of the Other Side, and to merit, in the World to Come, the four hundred worlds of longing, which are called the four hundred shekels of silver, current with the merchant.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:39: And further I heard that it is alluded to in the Name of forty-two letters, in the last word, "Shakotzit" - "tzit" in Aramaic translation means "hearing" - and the intent is that sackcloth causes prayer to be heard; and so "Shema Koleinu" ["hear our voice"] has the initial letters shin-kuf, [i.e.,] "sak."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:40: And my teacher, peace be upon him, wrote, concerning what they said in the Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas, page 227a), that "kash" [straw] and "teven" [chaff] are the husks, and "kesh" reversed is "sak" - and the intent is that since the penitent sinned and was drawn after the husk, it is fitting that he place sackcloth upon his flesh, and through this he subdues his inclination, which is the "straw."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:41: And I say, that concerning exile it is said (Isaiah 50:3), "I clothe the heavens with blackness, and I make sackcloth their covering" - behold, the Holy One, blessed be He, of whom it is said (1 Kings 8:32), "then You shall hear in heaven," is clothed in sackcloth. And of the Shechinah it is said (Joel 1:8), "lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth" - and since through his sin this person caused them to be clothed in sackcloth beyond what they should be - for when we sin, we prolong the exile and enthrone the sackcloth, which is the servant, more than is fitting - and likewise the whole soul is clothed in sackcloth, which is the husk - therefore, for the repair of the Shechinah and the repair of his soul, he shall place sackcloth upon himself, and especially in days of sorrow and weeping it is fitting to wear sackcloth.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:42: And behold, the reason for accepting suffering, fasting, weeping, and sackcloth is that the penitent, through his sin, caused a blemish above - and behold, that darkness depends on the supernal attributes, and through his accepting judgment upon himself, he purifies the supernal attributes from their blemish and darkness, for that judgment and darkness descend upon him [instead].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:43: And this matter we learn from Adam, the first man - for once he knew what he had blemished, he accepted upon himself the decree of judgment, and the supernal attributes were purified. And there is proof of this in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 69, page 99a), where he says there, on (Genesis 4:1), "and the man knew Chava his wife" - and until here Adam did not know his wife - rather, at the time he sinned, the Shechinah departed from her place, and so the masters of the Mishnah established, that at a time when the Shechinah is not in her place, marital relations are forbidden, and so on - and he caused that bed to depart from there, so he too departed from marital relations; and after he accepted his punishment, the bed returned to its place at that time, "and the man knew Chava his wife" - to this point. Behold, it is explicit that when he accepted the decree of his punishment, the attributes were repaired.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:44: And my teacher, peace be upon him, used to say that for this reason they instituted in the confession, "and You are righteous concerning all that has come upon me, for You have acted truthfully, and I have done wickedly" - and the intent is that in confessing his iniquity, he purifies the supernal attributes and brings down the darkness and blemish, which is the judgment, upon himself - and this is "and You are righteous concerning all that has come upon me" - "that has come," meaning both what has come and what will come. "For You have acted truthfully" - meaning, in the flowing of the judgment that shall come, the attribute of Truth is repaired, [since] "and I have done wickedly," and this is fitting for it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:45: And a further reason for accepting suffering is that one who transgresses a single sin acquires for himself a single accuser, who stands and accuses him always - and when a person confesses in the court of judgment, they abstain from him and he does not accuse. And so they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Kedoshim, page 83b) concerning David, when he said, "I have sinned," and the prophet said to him (2 Samuel 12:13), "the LORD also has removed your sin; you shall not die" - for this matter is difficult, since if the Holy One, blessed be He, removed his sin, why did David perform so many self-afflictions and fasts? Rather, according to what is explained there, it is resolved - that the intent is that He removed it from before the Holy One, blessed be He, so that it not accuse him. In these words: come and see, a person who performs a commandment - that commandment ascends and stands before the Holy One, blessed be He, and says, I am from so-and-so, who performed me - and the Holy One, blessed be He, appoints it before Him to watch over him every day, to do good to him because of it. One who transgresses the words of Torah - that transgression ascends before Him and says, I am from so-and-so, who performed me - and the Holy One, blessed be He, appoints it before Him, and it stands there to watch over him, to destroy him - this is what is written (Deuteronomy 32:19), "and the LORD saw it, and spurned them, because of the provocation of His sons and His daughters" - what is "and He saw"? That one which stands before Him. When he returns in repentance, what is written? (2 Samuel 12:13), "the LORD also has removed your sin; you shall not die" - that He removed that iniquity from before Him, so that He not gaze upon it, in order to do good to him. And concerning this it is written (Deuteronomy 9:27), "do not look upon the stubbornness of this people, nor their wickedness, nor their sin" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:46: Behold, that through iniquity a single accuser is created, and therefore one must accept suffering upon himself in order to cleanse his iniquities, as it is said (Psalms 89:33), "then I will visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with plagues" - and through this his iniquities are atoned for.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:47: And it appears to me that from the reason they said, of blessed memory (Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 11), that one who transgresses a single sin acquires for himself an accuser, may be understood what Onkelos translated: "sin" [chet] as "chova" [debt] (Numbers 18:22), "their sin" as "chovehon" (Exodus 32:32) - that the sin, which is the accuser, is a debt to the person, which he is obligated to pay. For in committing the iniquity, he borrows what is not his - for a person's nature is to be in holiness, and when he is drawn after the counsel of his inclination, behold, he owes it what he benefited from it, and how does he pay it back? By returning what he benefited from it, through the cleansing of suffering. And just as Gehinnom, the accusing force he created through his iniquity, comes and takes its vengeance from him - along the lines of what is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Korach (page 177a), "for the work of a man He shall repay him," and so on (Job 34:11) - in order to cleanse the impure force he drew upon his soul, so too in this world that impure force is cleansed through the acceptance of suffering, and once he completes the cleansing, that accuser is nullified - along the lines of what they said, of blessed memory (Sotah 9a), "arrows are vessels," and so on - for arrows exist only to do the will of the one who wields them, and once they have fulfilled his commands, they are nullified - and this is (Isaiah 44:22), "I have wiped away your transgressions like a thick cloud," and so on, "return to Me, for I have redeemed you" - and the intent is, I have redeemed you from those debts by which you were held.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:48: And therefore one must accept suffering out of love and not rebel against it - and so they expounded in the Mechilta (Parashat Yitro), on the verse (Exodus 20:20), "you shall not make with Me," in these words: Rabbi Akiva says, "you shall not make with Me" - that you not conduct yourselves with Me the way others conduct themselves with their gods - for when good comes upon them, they honor their gods, as it is said (Habakkuk 1:16), "therefore he sacrifices to his net"; and when punishment comes upon them, they curse their gods, as it is said (Isaiah 8:21), "and it shall come to pass, when he is hungry," and so on, "and he shall curse by his king." But if I bring good upon you, give thanks; and if I bring suffering upon you, give thanks. And so David said (Psalms 116:13), "I will lift up the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the LORD," (ibid. 116:3-4) "trouble and sorrow I found, and I called upon the name of the LORD." And so Job said (Job 1:21), "the LORD has given, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" - both for the attribute of good and the attribute of punishment. And so Job's wife said to him (ibid. 2:9), "do you still hold fast to your integrity?" - and what did he say to her? "You speak as one of the base women speaks." The generation of the Flood and the people of Sodom, who were accustomed to good, when punishment came upon them, accepted it against their will - but we, who are fitting in good, should we not be fitting in punishment too? And further, one should be more joyful in suffering than in good, for even if a person is in good all his days, the transgressions in his hand are not forgiven - and who forgives them? You must say, suffering.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:49: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says, behold it says (Proverbs 3:11), "my son, do not despise the discipline of the LORD" - why? "For whom the LORD loves, He corrects" - you might say, go and see who causes this son to please his father - you must say, this is suffering. Rabbi Meir says (Deuteronomy 8:5), "and you shall know in your heart that as a man chastens his son" - you shall know the deeds you have done, and the suffering I have brought upon you, that not according to your deeds have I brought suffering upon you [i.e., I have been lenient].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:50: Rabbi Natan says, suffering is precious, for just as a covenant is made with the land, so a covenant is made with suffering, as it is said (Deuteronomy 8:5), "the LORD your God chastens you," and it says, "for the LORD your God brings you into a good land." Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says, suffering is precious, for three gifts the Holy One, blessed be He, gave to Israel, and they were given only through suffering, and these are: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come. Torah, from where? As it is said (Proverbs 1:2), "to know wisdom and discipline, to understand words of understanding," and it is written (Psalms 94:12), "happy is the man whom You chasten, O Yah, and teach him out of Your Torah." The Land of Israel, from where? The text teaches, "the LORD your God chastens you," and it says, "for the LORD your God brings you into a good land." The World to Come, from where? The text teaches (Proverbs 6:23), "for the commandment is a lamp, and the Torah is light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way of life" - you might say, go and see which path brings a person to the life of the World to Come - you must say, this is suffering.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:51: Rabbi Nechemiah says, suffering is precious, for just as sacrifices bring favor, so suffering brings favor. Concerning sacrifices, what does it say (Leviticus 1:4)? "And it shall be accepted for him, to atone for him." Concerning suffering, what does it say (ibid. 26:43)? "And they shall accept their punishment [avonam]." And not only that, but suffering brings more favor than sacrifices, because sacrifices are through money, and suffering is through the body - and so it says (Job 2:4), "skin for skin, and all that a man has [he will give for his life]." And further they expounded there on the virtue of suffering, that even though Chizkiyahu taught Menasheh Torah, it did not benefit him at all, only suffering, as it is said (2 Chronicles 33:12), "and when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the LORD" - from here you learn that suffering is precious - to this point. Behold, in the virtue of suffering, that it atones for a person's iniquities, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:52: And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, expounded (Berachot 5a), in these words: and this is [in accord with] what Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish [said] - a covenant is stated concerning salt, and a covenant is stated concerning suffering. A covenant is stated concerning salt, as it is written (Leviticus 2:13), "and you shall not let the salt of the covenant of your God be lacking." And a covenant is stated concerning suffering (Deuteronomy 28:69), "these are the words of the covenant" - just as the covenant stated concerning salt: salt sweetens the meat, so the covenant stated concerning suffering: suffering cleanses all of a person's iniquities - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:53: And there in Berachot, after this discourse, the discourse of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is also brought: three gifts the Holy One, blessed be He, gave to Israel. And since it has come to our hand, let us say something about it: it is possible to say that these three gifts correspond to nefesh, ru'ach, and neshamah, and it is known that the root of these is placed in the sefirot - and the reason we place Torah before the Land of Israel is that Israel, before they merited the gift of the Land of Israel, merited the gift of the Torah in the wilderness, and before they merited it, it was through suffering - first (Exodus 14:10), "and Pharaoh drew near, and the children of Israel lifted up their eyes," and afterward the splitting of the Red Sea, and "they came to Marah, and could not drink the waters of Marah" (ibid. 15:23), and afterward at Rephidim, "and the people thirsted there for water" (ibid. 17:3), and afterward Amalek. And likewise, before they entered the land, Sichon and Og came against them. And likewise in the World to Come, "a river of fire flowed and came forth from before Him" (Daniel 7:10), and they explained in the Tikkunim (page 4a) that souls immerse in it, and so on - see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:54: And the reason they were given through suffering is that they are three "Elohim," as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit, page 31b), in these words: Rabbi Yosi said, what is the meaning of (Deuteronomy 4:7), "which has God so near to it" [Elohim kerovim]? It should have said "karov" [singular] - rather, supernal Elohim, Elohim of "the Fear of Isaac," lower Elohim - and therefore "kerovim" [plural]; and abundant might, which comes forth from one, and all are one - to this point. And behold, the Torah was given in fire, which is the second Elohim, of "the Fear of Isaac"; and likewise the Land of Israel is the lower Elohim, and the attribute of righteousness [Tzedek] lodges in it. And likewise the World to Come, which is the supernal Elohim. And therefore it is necessarily required that they come through suffering, so that that judgment flow downward, and be sweetened on the side of Chesed after the acceptance of judgment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:55: And they said they were given only through suffering, so that even a completely righteous man requires suffering to merit them. And so we find that Rashbi, peace be upon him, merited the wondrous wisdom only through the suffering he endured in the cave for thirteen years, as explained in Parashat Bereshit (Zohar, page 11b), and likewise in Tractate Shabbat (33b). And the reason is explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas, page 247a), whose words we copied in the Gate of Holiness (chapter 15), where he says: and further, there is a secret mingled with pressed olive oil - certainly the Torah is not mingled except for one who endures several afflictions for its sake, as the masters of the Mishnah established, that the Torah endures only in one who kills himself over it - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:56: And this allusion is alluded to in the Torah in another place, where it says (Exodus 27:20), "and they shall bring you pure olive oil, beaten, for the light" - for pure olive oil, which is the Torah, gives light only through beating, which is the crushing of matter - all the more so one who has iniquities, for in order to purify the blemish of the supernal attributes and the blemish of his soul, he must accept suffering in order to merit the World to Come or to merit Torah.
